display.title: Shehakol Nihyeh Bidvoro: Why a Drop of Water Gets Such a Big Brachah
display.summary_short: A Yiddish class for children on Yud-Aleph Shevat: the Rebbe's answer to why plain water gets the great brachah Shehakol, with a mashal about a cupcake, a baker and a farmer.
display.summary_long: Recorded live in Yiddish with a class of children on Yud-Aleph Shevat. The teacher opens with the brachah Shehakol and retells a question the Rebbe once asked at a children's rally in 770: why does a simple glass of water get the brachah 'everything came into being by His word', when an apple or a potato gets a brachah about where it grows? A mashal follows: a boy asks why he must make a brachah on a cupcake he already paid for. His father takes him to the baker and then to the farmer, and each one admits he was paid only for his work, not for the eggs, flour or wheat that Hashem created. A brachah is how we 'pay' Hashem and ask permission to enjoy His world. The Rebbe explained that a child might think he needs to ask permission for a nice apple, but not for a drop of water; so the brachah on water reminds us that everything, even a drop of water, comes from Hashem. Knowing that Hashem is always with us brings calm and joy. The teacher speaks about ours being the last generation of golus and the first of the Geulah, blesses the children for Yud-Aleph Shevat, and they say a brachah acharonah and sing a nigun. An informal conversation between adults closes the recording.
display.lesson: Every brachah, even on a drop of water, reminds us that everything comes from Hashem, and that He is with us all the time.

quality.notes: Live classroom recording. The nigun is transcribed as a repetition loop (about 10:00), and a second loop occurs in the final chat (about 11:02). The last two minutes are an informal adult conversation in Yiddish and English that names a private person.

other_personal.text: In the closing chat a speaker mentions her daughter asking whether she has a sister named Fraidy, a recently married Fraidy Kleiman; the answer is that it is another Kleiman, perhaps a cousin.
